title: Overtourism in 2027: Tourist Taxes, Caps and Booking Rules by Destination
metaDescription: Cities and parks are limiting visitor numbers and adding fees. A destination-by-destination guide to entry charges, booking requirements and timed slots.
excerpt: A growing list of famous places now require a ticket, a timed slot or a fee just to enter. Here is where, and what to book in advance.
author: Travel Editors
content:
For most of modern tourism's history, the answer to "can I visit?" was yes, always, for anyone who turned up. That is no longer universally true.

A growing number of destinations now require a paid ticket, a timed entry slot, or advance registration simply to enter — not a museum, the **place itself**. Others have capped daily numbers, banned new accommodation, or levied taxes steep enough to change behaviour.

None of this makes travel impossible. It makes it something you have to check before you go, which is a genuinely new requirement.

## Why This Is Happening

The underlying arithmetic is straightforward. Tourist numbers globally have grown faster than the capacity of the places people most want to see, and that demand concentrates extraordinarily narrowly — a handful of streets, a few viewpoints, a short season.

The consequences in affected places are concrete: housing converted to short-term rentals until locals cannot afford to live in the centre, shops replaced by souvenir outlets, infrastructure built for a town of fifty thousand serving several million a year, and physical erosion of sites that were not designed for the footfall.

The measures below are responses to that, and most were introduced after softer approaches failed.

## Destinations With Entry Fees or Access Charges

**Venice.** A day-visitor access fee applies on specified peak days, aimed at people visiting without staying overnight. Registration and payment in advance, with checks at entry points. Overnight guests are exempt but pay accommodation tax instead.

**Bali.** A tourist levy payable by all foreign visitors, best paid online before arrival. Spot checks occur at sites and at the airport — keep the receipt.

**Bhutan.** The long-standing Sustainable Development Fee, charged per night. The rate has varied significantly and there are discounted arrangements for Indian, Bangladeshi and Maldivian nationals.

**New Zealand and Iceland** have both applied or expanded visitor levies, typically collected at arrival or through accommodation.

**Most European cities** apply a per-person, per-night accommodation tax. Individually small, cumulatively noticeable for a family across a two-week trip, and frequently payable in cash at the property.

![Travel Trends travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1522623349500-de37a56ea2a5?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Destinations With Visitor Caps or Timed Entry

**Machu Picchu, Peru.** Strict daily limits, timed entry, defined circuits, and mandatory guides on some routes. Tickets regularly sell out weeks ahead in peak season.

**The Alhambra, Granada.** Timed entry to the Nasrid Palaces with a hard daily cap. Books out far in advance — this is the single most common "we got there and could not get in" experience in Spain.

**Acropolis, Athens.** Hourly visitor caps introduced to manage peak flow, with timed slots.

**Pompeii.** Daily visitor caps applied during peak periods.

**Sagrada Família, Barcelona.** Timed entry, sells out.

**Anne Frank House, Amsterdam.** Online-only tickets released on a rolling schedule. There is no walk-up option.

**Mount Fuji, Japan.** Trail fees and daily climber limits on the most popular route, with advance booking.

**Zion, Yosemite, Arches and several other US national parks.** Timed entry or vehicle reservation systems during peak months, booked through the national reservation system, often released in batches.

**Cinque Terre, Italy.** Trail cards required for the main coastal paths, with capacity management on the busiest sections.

**Uluru and Kakadu, Australia.** Park passes required in advance.

**Galápagos, Ecuador.** Visitor numbers tightly controlled, and most sites accessible only with a licensed guide.

**Komodo National Park, Indonesia.** Entry fee structures that have changed repeatedly — verify close to travel.

![Travel Trends travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1772116398473-77b4459c85f9?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Destinations Restricting Accommodation and Behaviour

**Barcelona** has moved to phase out short-term tourist rental licences over the coming years, which will change the accommodation market substantially.

**Amsterdam** has capped overnight stays, restricted new hotel development, moved some visitor activity out of the centre, and applies one of Europe's highest tourist taxes.

**Kyoto** has restricted access to parts of the Gion geisha district in response to harassment of maiko, with fines for photography on certain private streets. Take this seriously — it is a genuine and reasonable restriction, not a formality.

**Dubrovnik** limits cruise arrivals, restricts wheeled luggage in the old town at certain hours, and caps numbers inside the walls.

**Santorini** manages cruise passenger numbers on peak days.

**Mallorca, the Canaries and several Greek islands** have introduced or raised levies alongside restrictions on new tourist accommodation.

## What This Means for Planning

The old model — arrive, decide what to do, do it — no longer works reliably at the most famous sites. The new model has three steps:

**Check whether your destination requires anything in advance.** Search the official tourism board or national park site, not a third-party ticket reseller. Look specifically for the words "timed entry", "reservation required" or "visitor cap".

**Book the constrained things first**, before flights if necessary. If your trip's entire purpose is Machu Picchu or a specific trail, the permit determines the dates, not the other way round.

**Budget for the fees.** They are individually modest and collectively material. A family of four visiting several capped sites across a two-week European trip can easily spend a few hundred euros on entry alone.

**Beware unofficial resellers.** Where a site has a hard cap, third parties buy inventory and resell at a markup, and in some cases sell tickets that are not valid. Always start from the official site.

## The Better Response: Go Elsewhere, or Go at a Different Time

Every measure above exists because demand concentrates on a few places in a few weeks. The traveller's version of solving that is simple and rewarding:

- **Travel in shoulder season.** Most caps and fees bite hardest in peak months; many do not apply at all outside them.
- **Visit early or late in the day.** The crowd is a midday phenomenon almost everywhere.
- **Stay overnight rather than day-tripping.** Several schemes explicitly exempt overnight guests, because overnight visitors spend more and arrive less abruptly. You also get the place in the early morning, which is when it is worth seeing.
- **Go to the next town along.** Almost every over-visited destination has an under-visited equivalent within an hour, with the same landscape and none of the queue.

## A Practical Pre-Trip Check

Four weeks before any trip to a well-known destination, spend twenty minutes on this:

1. Does the destination itself charge an entry or tourist fee?
2. Do any of the sites we want require timed entry or advance booking?
3. Are any of them closed on the days we are there?
4. Is there a festival, holiday or event that will affect capacity?

Do it once, write the answers into the shared plan, and book what needs booking. It is a small amount of admin that prevents the specific, memorable disappointment of standing outside somewhere you flew a long way to see, reading a sign that says tickets must be bought online.

If you are planning with other people, this is the kind of task that gets assumed rather than assigned. Putting the bookings that need doing into a visible shared checklist — **Trypinn** keeps it next to the itinerary — means somebody actually does it.
